overview: The bias-variance tradeoff is a fundamental concept that describes how model complexity impacts prediction error. Understanding this tradeoff is essential for building models that generalize well.
This module covers bias vs variance, underfitting vs overfitting, learning curves, and regularization effects.

topics.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
theory: Bias is error due to overly simplistic assumptions — high bias models underfit data. Variance is error due to sensitivity to training data — high variance models overfit.
Total Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Error. As model complexity increases, bias decreases but variance increases.
The goal is finding the sweet spot that minimizes total error. This is the core of model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
visualIntuition: Interactive plot with X-axis as model complexity, Y-axis as error. Three curves: Bias², Variance, Total Error showing U-shaped total error.
visualSuggestions: Complexity slider with live error curve update
Decomposition animation showing bias vs variance contribution

code.content:
from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=500, n_features=1, noise=10)
model = DecisionTreeRegressor()
param_range = np.arange(1, 15)

train_scores, test_scores = validation_curve(
    model, X, y, param_name="max_depth", param_range=param_range,
    cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
)

train_mean = -np.mean(train_scores, axis=1)
test_mean = -np.mean(test_scores, axis=1)

plt.plot(param_range, train_mean, label="Training Error")
plt.plot(param_range, test_mean, label="Validation Error")
plt.xlabel("Model Complexity (max_depth)")
plt.ylabel("MSE")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Bias-Variance Tradeoff")
plt.show()

topics.title: Underfitting vs Overfitting
theory: Underfitting: Model too simple to capture data trends. Examples: linear model on non-linear data, high regularization.
Overfitting: Model too complex, memorizes noise in training data. Examples: very deep tree, polynomial of degree 15 on 20 points.
Good fit: Balance between bias and variance. Model captures true patterns without fitting noise.
visualIntuition: Three plots with same data: underfit (straight line through curve), good fit (smooth curve), overfit (wiggly line through all points).
visualSuggestions: Animated progression from underfit to overfit

code.description: Underfitting vs overfitting with polynomial regression
code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(1)
X = np.sort(5 * np.random.rand(80, 1), axis=0)
y = np.sin(X).ravel() + np.random.normal(0, 0.1, X.shape[0])

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))

for i, degree in enumerate([1, 4, 15]):
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree)
    X_poly = poly.fit_transform(X)
    model = LinearRegression().fit(X_poly, y)
    y_pred = model.predict(X_poly)
    
    plt.subplot(1, 3, i+1)
    plt.scatter(X, y, color="black", s=15)
    plt.plot(X, y_pred, color="red")
    plt.title(["Underfit (deg 1)", "Good Fit (deg 4)", "Overfit (deg 15)"][i])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

topics.title: Learning Curves
theory: Learning curves show model performance as a function of training set size. They help diagnose under/overfitting.
If train and validation scores converge at low value → underfitting (need more complex model). If gap stays large → overfitting (need more data or simpler model).
High bias: both curves plateau at high error. High variance: gap between curves, training error much lower than validation.
visualIntuition: Dual-line plot: training vs validation accuracy as training samples increase. Gap indicates overfitting, convergence at low value indicates underfitting.
visualSuggestions: Side-by-side comparison for different model complexities

code.content:
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=1000, n_features=20)
train_sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve(
    Ridge(), X, y, cv=5,
    train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10)
)

train_mean = np.mean(train_scores, axis=1)
val_mean = np.mean(val_scores, axis=1)

plt.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, label="Training Score")
plt.plot(train_sizes, val_mean, label="Validation Score")
plt.xlabel("Training Set Size")
plt.ylabel("Score")
plt.title("Learning Curve")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

topics.title: Regularization Effects
theory: Regularization penalizes model complexity to prevent overfitting. Adds penalty term to loss function.
L1 (Lasso): Shrinks some coefficients to exactly zero → feature selection. Good for sparse solutions.
L2 (Ridge): Shrinks all coefficients toward zero → smooth, stable solutions. Doesn't eliminate features.
Elastic Net combines both L1 and L2 regularization. Choice depends on problem and data characteristics.
visualIntuition: Bar plot of feature weights for Lasso vs Ridge. Slider for alpha parameter with real-time weight updates.
visualSuggestions: L1 vs L2 constraint region visualization

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=100, n_features=10, noise=10)

lasso = Lasso(alpha=0.1).fit(X, y)
ridge = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)

coef_indices = np.arange(len(ridge.coef_))

plt.bar(coef_indices - 0.2, ridge.coef_, width=0.4, alpha=0.7, label="Ridge (L2)")
plt.bar(coef_indices + 0.2, lasso.coef_, width=0.4, alpha=0.7, label="Lasso (L1)")
plt.xlabel("Feature Index")
plt.ylabel("Coefficient Value")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Regularization Effects on Coefficients")
plt.show()
